question: How do nurses know how much pain a patient is actually feeling?

options.A: By checking changes in blood pressure
options.B: By measuring the exact amount of tissue damage
options.C: By trusting whatever the patient says it is
options.D: By looking for visible redness and swelling

explanation: You've got this! Pain is entirely personal. Since we can't see or touch it directly, the patient's own word is always our best and most reliable guide. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why might two patients who had the exact same surgery report completely different pain levels?

options.A: One patient is always just exaggerating their discomfort
options.B: Hospital room temperatures change how nerves send distress signals
options.C: Surgical skill varies so much that tissue injury is never identical
options.D: Pain involves emotional and cultural factors, not just physical injury

explanation: Spot on! Pain isn't just about the physical cut. A person's emotions, background, and past experiences all change how they feel and express pain. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which nerve fibers send quick, sharp, 'ouch!' pain straight to your brain?
explanation: Great job! A-delta fibers are wrapped in myelin (like an insulated wire), letting them zoom signals to your brain instantly when you get hurt. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the main job of the body's modulation phase in the pain pathway?

options.A: Deciding the emotional meaning of the injury in the brain
options.B: Converting tissue injury into a nerve impulse
options.C: Releasing natural body chemicals to turn down the pain signal
options.D: Carrying the electrical message up the spinal cord

explanation: Think of modulation as your body's built-in volume control! It releases substances like endorphins right in the spinal cord to quiet down the pain message. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h2)

question: How long must pain stick around before it is officially called chronic pain?
explanation: You're doing great! While acute pain heals quickly, chronic pain hangs around long past the normal healing time—usually defined as lasting over 3 to 6 months. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h3)

question: A patient with long-term, poorly controlled diabetes complains of a burning, electric-shock feeling in their feet. What kind of pain is this?
explanation: Spot on! When nerves themselves get damaged (like from high blood sugar over time), they misfire, causing those classic burning, shooting, or electric sensations. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h3)

question: In the handy PQRSTU pain assessment tool, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?
explanation: Easy peasy! 'Q' stands for quality—asking the patient what the pain actually *feels* like (e.g., stabbing, dull, aching, or burning). [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h4)

question: Why might the standard 0-to-10 numeric pain scale be tricky to use for an adult with severe dementia?

options.A: Numeric scales only work for surgical wounds
options.B: Patients with dementia lose the ability to speak at all
options.C: They will always just say ten no matter what
options.D: They may struggle to connect a number to how they feel

explanation: Well reasoned! Numbers are abstract concepts. For patients with cognitive changes, we often need to rely on facial expression charts or physical behavior cues instead. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h4)

question: What is the most serious, life-threatening side effect nurses must watch out for when giving opioids?
explanation: You've got this! Opioids slow down the brain's breathing center, which is why checking the patient's respiratory rate is a vital nursing duty. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why is it crucial to keep track of a patient's total daily dose of paracetamol (acetaminophen)?

options.A: It causes rapid kidney failure within an hour
options.B: Too much of it can cause severe liver damage
options.D: Higher doses cause heavy stomach bleeding

explanation: Spot on! The liver breaks down paracetamol. If the daily limit is crossed, toxic byproducts build up and can cause serious liver injury. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the best immediate physical step to help reduce swelling right after a fresh injury?
explanation: Great clinical instinct! Cold constricts blood vessels, which slows down fluid pooling into the area and helps numb the sharp pain right away. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h6)

question: How do non-drug (non-pharmacological) methods help ease a patient's discomfort?

options.A: They permanently destroy local nerve endings
options.B: They chemically replace lost natural endorphins
options.C: They completely cure the underlying disease
options.D: They engage the mind and body to lower stress and pain signals

explanation: You're crushing it! Techniques like distraction, relaxation, and positioning don't just 'distract'—they actually trigger pathways in the nervous system that block pain signals. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h6)

question: What is the main difference between drug tolerance and psychological addiction?

options.A: Tolerance happens only in children; addiction happens in adults
options.B: Addiction is caused by paracetamol, tolerance by morphine
options.C: Tolerance means the drug stops working for any condition
options.D: Tolerance is a normal body adjustment needing higher doses, while addiction involves compulsive craving

explanation: Well explained! Tolerance just means your body gets used to a drug over time so you need a bit more for the same effect. Addiction is a complex behavioral drive to use drugs compulsively. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h7)

question: A patient taking strong opioids long-term for cancer pain complains of terrible constipation. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Proactively give prescribed stool softeners and laxatives
options.B: Tell the patient to stop drinking fluids
options.C: Stop the opioid medication immediately without telling the doctor
options.D: Tell the patient that opioids never cause constipation

explanation: Spot on! Opioids slow down bowel movements significantly. Since our bodies don't build tolerance to this side effect, preventative laxatives are a nursing must-have! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T7#GNS221_U3_T7_h7)
